Ingress & Egress

How outside traffic reaches Jahez apps on EKS — Ingress objects, IngressClass, the ingress-nginx controller, routing patterns, TLS with cert-manager — and how NetworkPolicy controls what leaves each Pod. Same structure as our Storage, Security, Helm and Kustomize guides.

jahez-prodme-central-1api.jahez.netmenu-apiorders-apiingress-nginx 1.15.0cert-managerNetworkPolicy

Part I · High Level

① Foundations — introduction, the need, the solution, comparisons. ② Architecture and workflows — where each part runs, the repo, what the controller does with one apply, and one request end to end. Small snippets here; full objects in Part II.

1

Foundations

1.1Introduction

In one sentence

An Ingress is a Kubernetes object that lists HTTP routing rules (host + path → Service). A separate program, the Ingress controller, reads those rules and turns them into a running reverse proxy behind one load balancer.

Definition

Ingress is a built-in API object, networking.k8s.io/v1 (stable since Kubernetes 1.19). It describes how HTTP and HTTPS requests from outside the cluster reach Services inside it: which host, which path, which Service and port, and which TLS certificate. It is pure configuration: the API server stores it, and nothing happens until an Ingress controller (ingress-nginx, AWS Load Balancer Controller, Traefik, F5 NGINX, Contour …) watches it and programs a proxy.

The Ingress API is frozen: it is supported and covered by CKAD, but new features go to its successor, the Gateway API. The community ingress-nginx controller used in this guide was retired in March 2026 (final releases v1.15.0, v1.14.4, v1.13.8). Existing installs keep working; there are no more fixes. §1.4 shows what to choose for new Jahez clusters.

Egress is the opposite direction: traffic leaving a Pod. Kubernetes has no “Egress object”; you control it with NetworkPolicy (policyTypes: [Egress]), enforced by the CNI (on EKS: the VPC CNI network-policy agent, or Calico / Cilium).

What it is — and what it is not

✓ It is
  • a routing table for HTTP(S): host + path → Service:port
  • declarative: you describe routes, the controller builds the proxy
  • the place for TLS termination (spec.tls → a kubernetes.io/tls Secret)
  • namespaced: it can only send traffic to Services in its own namespace
  • shared: many Ingress objects, many teams, one controller and one NLB
  • extended by annotations (rate limit, canary, rewrite) — controller-specific
✕ It is not
  • a Service type — Services are ClusterIP / NodePort / LoadBalancer; Ingress sits in front of them
  • a load balancer by itself — without a controller nothing listens
  • for TCP/UDP (Postgres, gRPC-over-TCP, MQTT) — HTTP(S) only
  • egress control — outbound traffic is NetworkPolicy’s job
  • the Gateway API — that is a different, newer set of objects (Gateway, HTTPRoute)
  • a firewall — NodePorts and other LoadBalancer Services can still bypass it

Definitions

①

Ingress (the object)

A YAML object of kind: Ingress that lists rules: “requests for this host and path go to this Service”.

🎯 Why it exists

Without it every app needs its own load balancer. The Ingress lets many apps share one entry point and describe their routes in git.

📄 What it looks like
📄 ingress/api-ingress.yamlyaml
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: api.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /menu
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: { name: menu-api-service, port: { number: 80 } }
⚙ What the controller / Kubernetes does with it

The API server validates and stores it in etcd. The controller sees the new object and adds a location /menu block for api.jahez.net to its proxy.

Before
GET https://api.jahez.net/menu
→ 404 (no rule)
→
After
GET https://api.jahez.net/menu
→ menu-api Pod 200
📍 Where it lives

① git ingress/ → ④ cluster, namespace jahez-prod (same namespace as the Services it points to).

⚠ Watch out

An Ingress cannot point to a Service in another namespace. Make one Ingress per namespace, or use an ExternalName Service (with care).

②

Ingress controller

A Deployment of proxy Pods (here: ingress-nginx) that watches Ingress objects and turns them into live proxy configuration.

🎯 Why it exists

The Ingress object is only data. Something must listen on :80/:443, terminate TLS and forward requests. Kubernetes ships no controller of its own.

📄 What it looks like
⌘ helm install (platform/ingress-nginx)bash
helm upgrade --install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  -n ingress-nginx --create-namespace \
  -f platform/ingress-nginx/values-prod.yaml --version 4.15.0
⚙ What the controller / Kubernetes does with it

Each controller Pod lists Ingresses, Services, EndpointSlices and Secrets, renders nginx.conf, reloads NGINX when routes change and updates Pod IPs live (no reload).

Before
Ingress api-ingress
ADDRESS: <empty>
→
After
Ingress api-ingress
ADDRESS: k8s-ingressn-….elb.me-central-1.amazonaws.com
📍 Where it lives

④ cluster, namespace ingress-nginx — 3 Pods spread over me-central-1a/b/c, behind one AWS NLB.

⚠ Watch out

ingress-nginx is retired (March 2026): no security fixes. Keep it patched at v1.15.0 and plan the move (§1.4). Never enable snippet annotations.

③

IngressClass

A small cluster-scoped object that names a controller. An Ingress picks its controller with spec.ingressClassName.

🎯 Why it exists

A cluster can run several controllers (public nginx, internal ALB). The class says which one owns which Ingress.

📄 What it looks like
📄 IngressClass nginxyaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: IngressClass
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  controller: k8s.io/ingress-nginx
⚙ What the controller / Kubernetes does with it

The controller ignores every Ingress whose ingressClassName is not its own class (and, unless told otherwise, Ingresses with no class at all).

Before
ingressClassName: (missing)
→ nobody serves it
→
After
ingressClassName: nginx
→ ingress-nginx serves it
📍 Where it lives

④ cluster-scoped (no namespace). Created by the Helm chart.

⚠ Watch out

The old annotation kubernetes.io/ingress.class is deprecated. Use the field. Marking a class default (is-default-class: "true") affects only Ingresses created afterwards.

④

Rule (host + path)

One entry in spec.rules: an optional host plus a list of paths, each sending to a backend.

🎯 Why it exists

One NLB serves many apps; the controller must decide per request. Host and path are the two things every HTTP request carries.

📄 What it looks like
📄 ruleyaml
- host: api.jahez.net
  http:
    paths:
      - path: /orders
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service: { name: orders-api-service, port: { number: 80 } }
⚙ What the controller / Kubernetes does with it

Becomes one NGINX server (per host) with one location (per path). Longest matching path wins.

Before
api.jahez.net/orders/42
→ no location
→
After
api.jahez.net/orders/42
→ orders-api-service:80
📍 Where it lives

Inside the Ingress, under spec.rules[].

⚠ Watch out

A rule with no host matches every host — including the raw NLB DNS name. Always set a host in production.

⑤

pathType

How the path is compared: Exact (whole path, case-sensitive), Prefix (by /-separated elements) or ImplementationSpecific (controller decides — regex in nginx).

🎯 Why it exists

Without a fixed rule, /menu might or might not match /menus. pathType makes matching predictable across controllers.

📄 What it looks like
📄 pathyaml
path: /menu
pathType: Prefix   # /menu, /menu/, /menu/items — not /menus
⚙ What the controller / Kubernetes does with it

The controller turns Prefix into a location that matches /menu and /menu/… only.

Before
Prefix /menu
/menus → ?
→
After
Prefix /menu
/menus → 404 (not matched)
📍 Where it lives

Required on every path in networking.k8s.io/v1.

⚠ Watch out

Regex (/v1/menu(/|$)(.*)) works only with ImplementationSpecific + use-regex. With Prefix it is rejected by the controller’s validation.

⑥

Backend Service

Where a matched request goes: a Service name and port (by number or by name) in the same namespace — or a resource backend (rare).

🎯 Why it exists

The Ingress never talks to Pods directly. The Service gives a stable name; the controller reads its EndpointSlices to find Pod IPs.

📄 What it looks like
📄 backendyaml
backend:
  service:
    name: menu-api-service
    port:
      name: http
⚙ What the controller / Kubernetes does with it

nginx sends straight to Pod IPs from the EndpointSlices (not through the ClusterIP). Pod changes update without a reload.

Before
Service has 0 ready endpoints
→
After
→ 503 Service Temporarily Unavailable
📍 Where it lives

Service in jahez-prod, usually type: ClusterIP.

⚠ Watch out

A wrong port name or a Service with no ready Pods gives 503, not 404. Check kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=….

⑦

TLS Secret

A Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls holding tls.crt and tls.key, named in spec.tls[].secretName.

🎯 Why it exists

HTTPS must end somewhere. Ending it at the controller means apps speak plain HTTP inside the cluster and certificates live in one place.

📄 What it looks like
📄 spec.tlsyaml
tls:
  - hosts: [api.jahez.net]
    secretName: api-jahez-net-tls-secret
⚙ What the controller / Kubernetes does with it

The controller loads the certificate and serves it by SNI for the listed hosts. cert-manager creates and renews the Secret.

Before
https://api.jahez.net
→ "Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate"
→
After
https://api.jahez.net
→ Let’s Encrypt cert, valid 90 days
📍 Where it lives

Same namespace as the Ingress.

⚠ Watch out

Missing or wrong Secret → the controller silently serves its fake self-signed certificate. Check events and kubectl get certificate.

⑧

defaultBackend

The backend for requests that match no rule in this Ingress.

🎯 Why it exists

Something must answer unknown paths. Without it the controller’s own default backend returns 404.

📄 What it looks like
📄 defaultBackendyaml
defaultBackend:
  service:
    name: menu-api-service
    port: { number: 80 }
⚙ What the controller / Kubernetes does with it

nginx uses it for the catch-all location of this Ingress’s hosts.

Before
GET /unknown
→ controller 404
→
After
GET /unknown
→ menu-api (its own 404 page)
📍 Where it lives

Inside the Ingress, spec.defaultBackend.

⚠ Watch out

An Ingress with only a defaultBackend and no rules catches all hosts on the controller — it can steal traffic from other teams.

⑨

Annotations

Key/values under metadata.annotations that tune the controller: rate limits, CORS, canary, rewrite, timeouts.

🎯 Why it exists

The Ingress spec only knows host, path, backend and TLS. Everything else is controller-specific and lives in annotations.

📄 What it looks like
📄 annotationsyaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "100"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
⚙ What the controller / Kubernetes does with it

The controller reads them while rendering the location and adds the matching NGINX directives.

Before
101st request/s from one IP
→ 200
→
After
101st request/s from one IP
→ 503 (limit-req)
📍 Where it lives

Inside the Ingress metadata.

⚠ Watch out

Values must be strings ("true", "100"). A typo is silently ignored. Annotations do not move to another controller — they are the main migration cost.

⑩

Egress

Traffic leaving a Pod: to another Pod, a database, DNS or the internet.

🎯 Why it exists

By default every Pod can reach everything. One compromised Pod could read every database or send data out.

📄 What it looks like
📄 the ideayaml
# menu-api may reach:  DNS:53, menu-db:5432
# everything else:    dropped
⚙ What the controller / Kubernetes does with it

Kubernetes has no Egress object. You write a NetworkPolicy with policyTypes: [Egress]; the CNI enforces it in the kernel.

Before
menu-api → orders-db:5432
→ connected
→
After
menu-api → orders-db:5432
→ timeout (dropped)
📍 Where it lives

Rules in network-policies/; enforced on every node.

⚠ Watch out

For a fixed source IP to the internet (payment gateway allow-lists) you need a NAT Gateway / egress gateway — NetworkPolicy only allows or drops.

⑪

NetworkPolicy

A namespaced object that selects Pods and lists who may connect to them (ingress) and where they may connect (egress).

🎯 Why it exists

Ingress controls the front door only. NetworkPolicy closes the side doors: Pod-to-Pod and Pod-to-database.

📄 What it looks like
📄 default denyyaml
kind: NetworkPolicy
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
⚙ What the controller / Kubernetes does with it

The CNI (VPC CNI policy agent, Calico, Cilium) turns it into eBPF / iptables rules on each node. Selected Pods become deny-by-default for the listed directions.

Before
no policy
→ all traffic allowed
→
After
default deny + allow rules
→ only listed traffic
📍 Where it lives

Namespace jahez-prod; enforced by the CNI on every node.

⚠ Watch out

If the CNI does not enforce policies (VPC CNI with the agent off, flannel), the objects are accepted and do nothing.

⑫

cert-manager

A controller that gets and renews TLS certificates (Let’s Encrypt via ACME) and stores them in TLS Secrets.

🎯 Why it exists

Certificates expire every 90 days. Renewing by hand across many hosts fails sooner or later.

📄 What it looks like
📄 annotation on the Ingressyaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod-cluster-issuer
⚙ What the controller / Kubernetes does with it

It sees the annotation, creates a Certificate, solves the ACME challenge (HTTP-01 through nginx or DNS-01 in Route 53) and writes the Secret.

Before
Secret api-jahez-net-tls-secret
→ missing
→
After
Secret api-jahez-net-tls-secret
→ tls.crt + tls.key, auto-renewed
📍 Where it lives

④ cluster, namespace cert-manager; ClusterIssuer is cluster-scoped.

⚠ Watch out

HTTP-01 needs DNS already pointing at the NLB and port 80 open. Wildcards need DNS-01.

1.2Problems or needs

In one sentence

Before Ingress, every app that must be reached from outside gets its own type: LoadBalancer Service — its own AWS NLB, its own DNS name and port, no shared TLS, and every Pod can still reach every database.

Step 1 of 6 · Expose menu-api
Where② AWS + ④ clusterWhoyouCommandkubectl apply
  • The mobile app needs the menu. The quick way: change menu-api’s Service to type: LoadBalancer.
  • The AWS Load Balancer Controller creates NLB #1, listening on :38080, forwarding to NodePort 30080 on every node.
  • Customers reach it at http://k8s-jahezpro-menuapil-….elb.me-central-1.amazonaws.com:38080.
⎈ Full cluster · Before Ingress — one NLB per app
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Customer app → NLB · menu → kube-proxy → menu-api Pods
📄 before/menu-api-lb-service.yamlyaml
# before/menu-api-lb-service.yaml — the old way: one NLB per app
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-api-lb-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: external
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: instance
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer           # ⚠ a dedicated AWS NLB for this app
  selector:
    app: menu-api
  ports:
    - port: 38080              # ⚠ users must know the port
      targetPort: 8080
      nodePort: 30080          # ⚠ open on every node
⌘ commandsbash
kubectl apply -f before/menu-api-lb-service.yaml
kubectl get svc menu-api-lb-service -n jahez-prod -w
▤ example outputoutput
NAME                  TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP                                         PORT(S)           AGE
menu-api-lb-service   LoadBalancer   172.20.41.17   k8s-jahezpro-menuapil-1a2b3c.elb.me-central-1.amazonaws.com   38080:30080/TCP   2m
Step 2 of 6 · Expose orders-api
Where② AWS + ④ clusterWhoyouCommandkubectl apply
  • orders-api needs the same, so it gets NLB #2 on :38282.
  • Now the app has two hostnames and two ports to remember, and AWS bills two NLBs (hourly + traffic).
  • Add 20 more services (search, cart, payments, vendor portal …) and you have 20 NLBs and 20 DNS records.
⎈ Full cluster · Before Ingress — one NLB per app
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Customer app → NLB · menu → NLB · orders → kube-proxy → menu-api Pods → orders-api Pods
📄 before/orders-api-lb-service.yamlyaml
# before/orders-api-lb-service.yaml — a second NLB, a second DNS name
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-api-lb-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: external
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: instance
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer           # ⚠ second NLB
  selector:
    app: orders-api
  ports:
    - port: 38282
      targetPort: 8080
      nodePort: 30282
⌘ commandsbash
kubectl apply -f before/orders-api-lb-service.yaml
kubectl get svc -n jahez-prod -o wide
▤ example outputoutput
NAME                    TYPE           EXTERNAL-IP                                           PORT(S)
menu-api-lb-service     LoadBalancer   k8s-jahezpro-menuapil-1a2b3c.elb.me-central-1.amazonaws.com   38080:30080/TCP
orders-api-lb-service   LoadBalancer   k8s-jahezpro-ordersap-4d5e6f.elb.me-central-1.amazonaws.com   38282:30282/TCP
Step 3 of 6 · Add DNS by hand
Where① Route 53WhoyouCommandaws route53
  • Each NLB has a random AWS name, so you add one Route 53 record per app.
  • Every new service = a new record, a new load balancer, a new port in the mobile app config.
  • If an NLB is re-created (Service deleted by mistake) its name changes and the record breaks.
⎈ Full cluster · Before Ingress — one NLB per app
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Customer app → Route 53 → NLB · menu → NLB · orders
⌘ commandsbash
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ \
  --change-batch file://menu-cname.json      # menu.jahez.net   → NLB #1
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ \
  --change-batch file://orders-cname.json    # orders.jahez.net → NLB #2
dig +short menu.jahez.net orders.jahez.net
▤ example outputoutput
k8s-jahezpro-menuapil-1a2b3c.elb.me-central-1.amazonaws.com.
15.185.10.21
k8s-jahezpro-ordersap-4d5e6f.elb.me-central-1.amazonaws.com.
15.185.77.140
Step 4 of 6 · TLS in every app
Where④ every PodWhoeach teamCommandopenssl / curl
  • The NLBs only pass TCP. HTTPS must be done inside each app (Kestrel certificates) or not at all.
  • Each team buys, mounts and renews its own certificate — or ships plain HTTP. Tokens and order data travel in clear text.
  • No shared place for HSTS, redirects, CORS or rate limits.
⎈ Full cluster · Before Ingress — one NLB per app
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Customer app → NLB · menu → menu-api Pods → orders-api Pods
⌘ commandsbash
curl -sv http://menu.jahez.net:38080/menu/categories 2>&1 | grep -E "^> |^< HTTP"
curl -sv https://menu.jahez.net:38080/ 2>&1 | tail -1
▤ example outputoutput
> GET /menu/categories HTTP/1.1
> Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi…        ← token in clear text
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
curl: (35) error:0A00010B:SSL routines::wrong version number
Step 5 of 6 · Every Pod reaches every DB
Where④ jahez-prod → jahez-dataWhonobody controls itCommandkubectl exec
  • Kubernetes allows all Pod-to-Pod traffic by default. menu-api can open orders-db; any Pod can call the internet.
  • One vulnerable dependency in menu-api = access to every database (lateral movement).
  • NodePorts 30080 / 30282 are open on every node’s IP as a side door around any proxy.
⎈ Full cluster · Before Ingress — one NLB per app
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: menu-api Pods → menu-db-0 → orders-db-0
⌘ commandsbash
kubectl exec -n jahez-prod deploy/menu-api-deployment -- \
  nc -zv -w 3 orders-db.jahez-data.svc.cluster.local 5432
kubectl get networkpolicy -A
▤ example outputoutput
orders-db.jahez-data.svc.cluster.local (172.20.88.12:5432) open      ← menu-api should never reach this
No resources found
Step 6 of 6 · Add it up
WhereeverywhereWhoplatform teamCommandkubectl get svc -A
  • N public apps = N NLBs, N DNS records, N ports, N certificates — and zero shared observability or rate limiting.
  • Nothing stops traffic between Pods or out of the cluster.
  • What we need: one entry point, routing by host and path, TLS in one place, and allow-lists for traffic between Pods. That is §1.3.
⎈ Full cluster · Before Ingress — one NLB per app
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Customer app → Route 53 → NLB · menu → NLB · orders → kube-proxy → menu-api Pods → orders-api Pods → menu-db-0 → orders-db-0
⌘ commandsbash
kubectl get svc -A --field-selector spec.type=LoadBalancer
▤ example outputoutput
NAMESPACE    NAME                    TYPE           EXTERNAL-IP
jahez-prod   menu-api-lb-service     LoadBalancer   k8s-jahezpro-menuapil-1a2b3c.elb…
jahez-prod   orders-api-lb-service   LoadBalancer   k8s-jahezpro-ordersap-4d5e6f.elb…
jahez-prod   search-api-lb-service   LoadBalancer   k8s-jahezpro-searchap-7a8b9c.elb…
… (one per public app)

How Ingress solves each one → 1.3

#ProblemWhat breaks
P1One NLB per appcost grows per service; quota of load balancers per region
P2One DNS name + port per appmobile config per service; records break when an NLB is re-created
P3TLS inside every appplain HTTP or N certificates to renew by hand
P4No shared edge featuresrate limit, CORS, redirects, canary re-done (or skipped) per team
P5No Pod isolationany Pod reaches any DB or the internet
P6NodePorts on every nodeside doors around any future proxy

1.3Solution

In one sentence

Install one Ingress controller behind one NLB, make every app Service ClusterIP, describe routes in Ingress objects, let cert-manager handle certificates, and close Pod-to-Pod traffic with NetworkPolicies.

The solution in 6 steps

  1. Install the controller once — helm upgrade --install ingress-nginx with values-prod.yaml: 3 Pods across 3 zones, one LoadBalancer Service → one AWS NLB.
  2. Point DNS once — api.jahez.net, menu.jahez.net, orders.jahez.net, partners.jahez.com are all aliases of the same NLB.
  3. Make app Services internal — menu-api-service and orders-api-service become type: ClusterIP. No NodePorts.
  4. Write the routes — api-ingress: api.jahez.net/menu → menu-api, /orders → orders-api, plus rate limit and CORS annotations.
  5. Automate TLS — cert-manager reads cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer, gets a Let’s Encrypt certificate into api-jahez-net-tls-secret and renews it.
  6. Close the side doors — default-deny NetworkPolicy, then allow only ingress-nginx → apps and each app → its own database.
⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path

1.4Comparisons

In one sentence

Ingress is one of four ways to let traffic in. Pick it for HTTP(S) apps sharing one entry point; pick the Gateway API for new platforms; pick a LoadBalancer Service for raw TCP.

Ingress vs Egress

Dimension📥 Ingress📤 Egress
Directionoutside → cluster (inbound)Pod → anywhere (outbound)
Kubernetes objectkind: Ingress (networking.k8s.io/v1)kind: NetworkPolicy with policyTypes: [Egress]
Enforced byIngress controller Pods (a proxy)the CNI on each node (eBPF / iptables)
LayerL7 — HTTP / HTTPSL3/L4 — IP, port, protocol
Defaultnothing from outside reaches a ClusterIP Serviceeverything allowed until a policy selects the Pod
TLSterminated at the controllernot involved (traffic passes as is)
Rate limitingyes — per IP, per Ingress (annotations)no — allow or drop only
Can be bypassed?yes, if NodePorts or other LoadBalancer Services existno — enforced in the node kernel (if the CNI supports it)
ObservabilityPrometheus metrics per host / path / statuspolicy verdict logs (VPC CNI / Calico flow logs)
Fixed outbound IP—not NetworkPolicy: NAT Gateway or egress gateway

NodePort vs LoadBalancer vs Ingress vs Gateway API

NodePort ServiceLoadBalancer ServiceIngressGateway API
LayerL4L4 (NLB)L7 HTTP(S)L4 + L7 (HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute, TLSRoute…)
Load balancersnone (node IPs)one per Serviceone per controllerone per Gateway
Routing by host/path✕✕✓✓ plus headers, methods, query
TLS termination✕NLB TLS listener (ACM) only✓ spec.tls✓ on the Gateway listener
Traffic split / canary✕✕annotations (controller-specific)✓ built in (weight)
Roles——one object for infra + appGateway (platform) vs Route (app team)
Status (Nov 2026)stablestablestable, feature-frozen; CKAD topicGA, actively developed — the successor
Jahez usedebugging onlythe controller itself; TCP (e.g. MQTT)existing HTTP apps (this guide)new clusters / migration target
⚠ ingress-nginx is retired (March 2026)

The Kubernetes project stopped maintaining the community ingress-nginx controller in March 2026: no more releases, bug fixes or security patches. Installs keep running and the Helm chart stays downloadable. The Ingress API itself is still supported. This guide uses ingress-nginx because its annotations are what CKAD tasks and most existing clusters use. For new Jahez clusters, choose one of the options below.

Controllers compared

ControllerRunsStatusStrengthsWatch out
ingress-nginx (kubernetes/ingress-nginx)NGINX Pods behind an NLBretired Mar 2026 (final v1.15.0)huge annotation set, canary, rewrite, CKAD examplesno security fixes; snippets were the 2025 CVE vector
AWS Load Balancer Controllerno proxy Pods — one ALB per IngressGroupmaintained by AWSnative on EKS: ACM certs, WAF, Cognito, target type ipdifferent annotations; no regex rewrite; ALB per group costs
F5 NGINX Ingress ControllerNGINX Podsmaintained by F5 (OSS + Plus)NGINX-based, VirtualServer CRDs, Gateway API supportdifferent annotation prefix (nginx.org/)
TraefikTraefik Podsmaintainedreads many ingress-nginx annotations (migration aid), Gateway APIown middleware CRDs for advanced cases
Envoy Gateway / Contour / IstioEnvoy PodsmaintainedGateway API first, retries, mTLS, rich traffic splitnew objects to learn (Gateway, HTTPRoute)

When to choose something else

  • Raw TCP / UDP (Postgres for a vendor, MQTT for courier devices) → a LoadBalancer Service or a Gateway TCPRoute.
  • New cluster or a big redesign → Gateway API (Envoy Gateway, or AWS Gateway API controller). Convert existing Ingresses with ingress2gateway (1.0 released March 2026).
  • AWS-native edge (WAF, Shield, ACM, Cognito) → AWS Load Balancer Controller with ingressClassName: alb.
  • Lift and shift with minimal YAML change → keep the Ingress objects, change ingressClassName to another controller and re-map annotations; run both controllers side by side first.

In one sentence

A request crosses four locations — the internet, AWS, the controller namespace and the app namespace — and three controllers (ingress-nginx, cert-manager, AWS Load Balancer Controller) keep those locations in sync with your YAML.

Every component

☁️ AWS NLB

What
The single public entry point. Listens on :80/:443 in three AZs and forwards TCP to controller Pod IPs.
Created by
AWS Load Balancer Controller, from the controller’s LoadBalancer Service
Key facts
nlb-target-type: ip · externalTrafficPolicy: Local keeps the client IP · one per cluster

⎈ Ingress controller (nginx)

What
NGINX + Lua inside each Pod. Watches the API and rewrites nginx.conf; per request: TLS → rate limit → CORS → match host/path → proxy → metrics.
Created by
Helm chart ingress-nginx 4.15.0
Key facts
3–9 replicas (HPA) · topology spread by zone · metrics on :10254 · reload without dropping connections

📋 Ingress object

What
Your routing table: host + path → Service:port, TLS, annotations.
Created by
you (git → Argo CD)
Key facts
namespaced · validated by the controller’s admission webhook before it is stored

🔐 cert-manager

What
Gets certificates from Let’s Encrypt (ACME), stores them in TLS Secrets, renews 30 days before expiry.
Created by
Helm chart jetstack/cert-manager
Key facts
HTTP-01 through nginx for single hosts · DNS-01 via Route 53 for wildcards

🛡️ NetworkPolicy engine

What
Turns NetworkPolicies into kernel rules on every node.
Created by
EKS VPC CNI with enableNetworkPolicy: "true" (or Calico / Cilium)
Key facts
deny-by-default once a Pod is selected · flannel does not enforce policies

🔗 ClusterIP Services

What
Stable names for the apps. Internal only; the controller reads their EndpointSlices and proxies straight to Pod IPs.
Created by
you
Key facts
no NodePort, no NLB per app — the Ingress is the only way in

# platform/namespaces.yaml — the four namespaces this guide uses
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: ingress-nginx          # the controller lives here
  labels:
    jahez.net/tier: edge
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: cert-manager           # issues and renews TLS certificates
  labels:
    jahez.net/tier: platform
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: jahez-prod             # menu-api, orders-api and their Ingresses
  labels:
    jahez.net/tier: apps
    env: prod
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: jahez-data             # menu-db, orders-db, redis
  labels:
    jahez.net/tier: data
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: jahez-prod-resource-quota
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "20"
    requests.memory: 40Gi
    limits.cpu: "40"
    limits.memory: 80Gi
    pods: "120"

helm valuesplatform/ingress-nginx/values-prod.yaml
In one sentence

Helm values for the controller: its class, 3+ replicas across zones, one AWS NLB, global NGINX settings and metrics.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: jahez-gitops → kubectl · helm → ConfigMap → AWS NLB
📄 values-prod.yamlyaml
# platform/ingress-nginx/values-prod.yaml
# helm upgrade --install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
#   -n ingress-nginx -f platform/ingress-nginx/values-prod.yaml --version 4.15.0
controller:
  # ① Which class does this controller own?
  ingressClass: nginx
  ingressClassResource:
    name: nginx                    # IngressClass object the chart creates
    enabled: true
    default: false                 # every Ingress must say ingressClassName: nginx
    controllerValue: k8s.io/ingress-nginx
  watchIngressWithoutClass: false

  # ② How many copies, and where?
  replicaCount: 3
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone    # me-central-1a/b/c
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx
          app.kubernetes.io/component: controller
  resources:
    requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
    limits: { memory: 512Mi }
  autoscaling:
    enabled: true
    minReplicas: 3
    maxReplicas: 9
    targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70

  # ③ How does traffic reach it? (one AWS NLB for the whole cluster)
  service:
    type: LoadBalancer
    externalTrafficPolicy: Local             # keep the client IP
    annotations:
      service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: external
      service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
      service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
      service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled: "true"

  # ④ Global behaviour (rendered into the controller ConfigMap)
  config:
    use-forwarded-headers: "true"
    hsts: "true"
    hsts-max-age: "31536000"
    proxy-body-size: 8m
    enable-real-ip: "true"
    log-format-escape-json: "true"
  allowSnippetAnnotations: false             # snippets stay off (CVE-2025-1974 family)

  # ⑤ Metrics for Prometheus / Grafana
  metrics:
    enabled: true
    serviceMonitor:
      enabled: true
What each block does
① class
the chart creates IngressClass nginx; not default, so every Ingress must name it
② copies
one Pod per zone minimum, HPA up to 9
③ service
one NLB, target type ip, client IP kept
④ config
goes into the controller ConfigMap (HSTS, body size, real IP)
⑤ metrics
ServiceMonitor for Prometheus

📄 ingress-class.yamlyaml
# What the chart creates from controller.ingressClassResource (shown for reference)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: IngressClass
metadata:
  name: nginx                                   # chart-owned name, kept as is
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx
  annotations:
    ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "false"
spec:
  # ① Which controller implements this class?
  controller: k8s.io/ingress-nginx
  # ② Extra controller settings (optional, controller-specific)
  # parameters:
  #   apiGroup: k8s.example.com
  #   kind: IngressParameters
  #   name: external-lb-parameters
  #   scope: Cluster
What each block does
controller
must equal the controller’s --controller-class
is-default-class
"false": Ingresses without a class are ignored

ClusterIssuerplatform/cert-manager/cluster-issuer.yaml
In one sentence

Tells cert-manager how to get certificates from Let’s Encrypt: HTTP-01 through nginx for normal hosts, DNS-01 in Route 53 for wildcards.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: ClusterIssuer → kubectl · helm
📄 cluster-issuer.yamlyaml
# platform/cert-manager/cluster-issuer.yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod-cluster-issuer
spec:
  acme:
    # ① Which certificate authority?
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: platform@jahez.net
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-account-key-secret
    # ② How do we prove we own the domain?
    solvers:
      - http01:                          # single hosts: api.jahez.net …
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: nginx
      - selector:
          dnsZones:
            - jahez.net                  # wildcards need DNS-01
        dns01:
          route53:
            region: me-central-1
            hostedZoneID: Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ
What each block does
① CA
production ACME endpoint + contact email + account key Secret
② solvers
HTTP-01 for any host; DNS-01 only for names in the jahez.net zone

Deploymentapps/menu-api/deployment.yaml
In one sentence

menu-api Pods: 3 replicas across zones, serving under /menu on port 8080, with readiness probes the controller relies on.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: jahez-gitops → kubectl · helm → menu-api Pods
📄 deployment.yamlyaml
# apps/menu-api/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-api-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: menu-api
    version: "2.14.0"
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-api
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: menu-api
      annotations:
        prometheus.io/scrape: "true"
        prometheus.io/port: "9090"
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: menu-api
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
      containers:
        - name: menu-api
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-api:2.14.0
          ports:
            - { name: http, containerPort: 8080 }
            - { name: metrics, containerPort: 9090 }
          env:
            - name: ASPNETCORE_PATHBASE          # app serves under /menu
              value: /menu
            - name: ConnectionStrings__MenuDb
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: menu-api-secret
                  key: menu-db-connection
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
            limits: { memory: 512Mi }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /menu/health/ready, port: http }
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /menu/health/live, port: http }
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities: { drop: [ALL] }
What each block does
ASPNETCORE_PATHBASE
the app expects the /menu prefix, so the Ingress needs no rewrite
readinessProbe
only Ready Pods enter the EndpointSlice → only they get traffic

In one sentence

Scales menu-api between 3 and 12 Pods on CPU and keeps 2 available during node drains.

# apps/menu-api/hpa-pdb.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: menu-api-hpa
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: menu-api-deployment
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 12
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 }
  behavior:
    scaleDown: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300 }
    scaleUp: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 30 }
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: menu-api-pdb
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-api
What each block does
HPA
scale up fast (30 s), down slowly (5 min)
PDB
drains wait until 2 Pods stay Ready

Ingressingress/api-ingress.yaml
In one sentence

The main entry: api.jahez.net/menu → menu-api, /orders → orders-api, TLS from cert-manager, rate limit and CORS.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Ingress ×5 → kubectl · helm → ingress-nginx controller Pods
📄 api-ingress.yamlyaml
# ingress/api-ingress.yaml — one host, two paths, TLS, rate limit
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/part-of: jahez-api
  annotations:
    # ── controller behaviour for this Ingress only ──
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod-cluster-issuer
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "100"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections: "20"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/enable-cors: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/cors-allow-origin: "https://www.jahez.net"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "30"
spec:
  # ① Which controller should serve it?
  ingressClassName: nginx

  # ② Which requests? (host + path)
  rules:
    - host: api.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - # ③ Where to send /menu…?
            path: /menu
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port:
                  name: http
          - # ③ Where to send /orders…?
            path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-api-service
                port:
                  number: 80

  # ④ How is it secured?
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - api.jahez.net
      secretName: api-jahez-net-tls-secret

  # ⑤ What about everything else?
  defaultBackend:
    service:
      name: menu-api-service
      port:
        number: 80
What each block does
① ingressClassName
served by ingress-nginx
② rules
one host, two Prefix paths
③ backend
Service by port name and by port number
④ tls
Secret created by cert-manager (annotation)
⑤ defaultBackend
unknown paths go to menu-api

kubectl apply -f ingress/api-ingress.yaml

Subdomain routing plus a wildcard host, covered by one wildcard certificate.

📄 subdomains-ingress.yamlyaml
# ingress/subdomains-ingress.yaml — one subdomain per app, one wildcard certificate
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: subdomains-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "200"
spec:
  # ① Which controller?
  ingressClassName: nginx
  # ② Which requests?
  rules:
    - host: menu.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port: { number: 80 }
    - host: orders.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-api-service
                port: { number: 80 }
    - host: "*.preview.jahez.net"           # wildcard: one label only
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port: { number: 80 }
  # ④ Secured by one wildcard certificate (DNS-01, see §6.2)
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - menu.jahez.net
        - orders.jahez.net
        - "*.preview.jahez.net"
      secretName: wildcard-jahez-net-tls-secret
What each block does
rules
one rule per host
*.preview.jahez.net
matches exactly one extra label
tls
Secret from the explicit Certificate in tls/

Ingressingress/legacy-rewrite-ingress.yaml
In one sentence

Keeps old mobile builds working: /v1/menu/… is rewritten to /menu/….

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Ingress ×5 → kubectl · helm → ingress-nginx controller Pods
📄 legacy-rewrite-ingress.yamlyaml
# ingress/legacy-rewrite-ingress.yaml — /v1/menu/<rest> reaches menu-api as /menu/<rest>
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: legacy-rewrite-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/use-regex: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /menu/$2
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: api.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /v1/menu(/|$)(.*)            # $1 = "/" or end, $2 = the rest
            pathType: ImplementationSpecific   # regex needs this type
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port: { number: 80 }

Ingressingress/orders-canary-ingress.yaml
In one sentence

Sends 5 % of api.jahez.net/orders (and every request with X-Canary: always) to orders-api 3.9.0.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path

Lit: orders-api-canary → kubectl · helm → ingress-nginx controller Pods
📄 orders-canary-ingress.yamlyaml
# ingress/orders-canary-ingress.yaml — 5 % of /orders traffic goes to v3.9.0
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: orders-canary-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "5"
    # header wins over weight: QA sends X-Canary: always
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-header: X-Canary
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: api.jahez.net            # same host + path as api-ingress
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-api-canary-service
                port: { number: 80 }
What each block does
canary: "true"
marks this Ingress as a canary of the main one with the same host + path
canary-weight
0–100 share of traffic
canary-by-header
always / never override the weight

Certificatetls/wildcard-jahez-net-certificate.yaml
In one sentence

Explicit Certificate for the subdomain Ingress (wildcards cannot use the annotation shortcut with HTTP-01).

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Certificate → kubectl · helm → TLS Secrets
📄 wildcard-jahez-net-certificate.yamlyaml
# tls/wildcard-jahez-net-certificate.yaml — explicit Certificate (wildcard needs DNS-01)
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: wildcard-jahez-net-certificate
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which names?
  dnsNames:
    - menu.jahez.net
    - orders.jahez.net
    - "*.preview.jahez.net"
  # ② Who signs it?
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-prod-cluster-issuer
    kind: ClusterIssuer
  # ③ Where is it stored?
  secretName: wildcard-jahez-net-tls-secret
  # ④ When is it renewed?
  duration: 2160h       # 90 days (Let's Encrypt maximum)
  renewBefore: 720h     # renew 30 days before expiry
  privateKey:
    algorithm: ECDSA
    size: 256
    rotationPolicy: Always
What each block does
① dnsNames
every name in the certificate
② issuerRef
the ClusterIssuer
③ secretName
what the Ingress names in spec.tls
④ duration / renewBefore
90 days, renewed at day 60

In one sentence

Only ingress-nginx controller Pods may open port 8080 on menu-api and orders-api.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen

📄 allow-ingress-nginx.yamlyaml
# network-policies/allow-ingress-nginx.yaml — only the controller may call the apps
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-ingress-nginx-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which Pods?
  podSelector:
    matchExpressions:
      - key: app
        operator: In
        values: [menu-api, orders-api]
  # ② Which direction?
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  # ③ Who may come in?
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:              # AND: same list item
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
What each block does
from: namespaceSelector + podSelector
one list item = AND
ports
containerPort 8080, not the Service port 80

# network-policies/menu-api-egress.yaml — DNS + menu-db only
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: menu-api-egress-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which Pods?
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: menu-api
  # ② Which direction?
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  # ④ Where may they go?
  egress:
    - # DNS to CoreDNS
      to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
    - # menu-db only — orders-db is not listed, so it is blocked
      to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-data
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: menu-db
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
What each block does
DNS rule
without it every name lookup times out
menu-db rule
orders-db is not listed, so it is blocked

# network-policies/orders-api-egress.yaml — DNS + orders-db + Redis + payment gateway
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-api-egress-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-api
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-data
          podSelector:
            matchExpressions:
              - key: app
                operator: In
                values: [orders-db, redis]
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 6379 }
    - # payment gateway — outside the cluster, by CIDR

        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 203.0.113.0/24
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 443 }

for destinations outside the cluster

2.3Inside the controller — from apply to live route

In one sentence

Every Ingress change goes through the same nine stages: you run a command, the API server validates and stores it, and the controller filters by class, resolves Services and Secrets, renders nginx.conf, reloads only if needed and writes the NLB address back.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: jahez-gitops → kubectl · helm → kube-apiserver → admission webhook (inside the controller Pod) → etcd → ingress-nginx controller Pods → IngressClass nginx → menu-api-service → orders-api-service → EndpointSlices → cert-manager → TLS Secrets → Ingress ×5

Part II · Low Level

Details and depth: every object field by field, routing patterns, TLS, NetworkPolicy and every command.

3

The Ingress object

Object by object, logic first: the question each field answers, one full YAML grouped by those questions, then every property as a tree.

3.0How an Ingress works

In one sentence

An Ingress is a list of rules — host + path → Service:port — plus TLS and a fallback, addressed to one controller through its IngressClass.

An Ingress answers five questions in a fixed order. Read the YAML top to bottom and you read the questions top to bottom.

Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
① Which controller should serve it?ingressClassNamethe post office this letter is addressed to
② Which requests? (host + path)rules[].host · rules[].http.paths[].path · pathTypethe address on the envelope
③ Where to send them?paths[].backend.service.name · port.number | port.namethe flat inside the building
④ How is it secured?tls[].hosts · tls[].secretNamethe sealed envelope
⑤ What about everything else?defaultBackendthe reception desk for unknown names
Familynetworking.k8s.io/v1
Scopenamespaced
Short nameing
Survivesuntil deleted; routes vanish with it
Typical useHTTP(S) entry for ClusterIP Services
⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Customer app → Ingress ×5 → ingress-nginx controller Pods → menu-api-service → orders-api-service → EndpointSlices

Structure

📄 structuretext
Ingress
├── metadata (name · namespace · annotations)
└── spec
    ├── ① ingressClassName
    ├── ② rules[]
    │     ├── host
    │     └── http.paths[]
    │           ├── path · pathType
    │           └── ③ backend → service{name, port} | resource
    ├── ④ tls[] → hosts[] · secretName
    └── ⑤ defaultBackend → service | resource
status.loadBalancer.ingress[]   ← written by the controller

Full YAML — every field

📄 ingress/api-ingress.yamlyaml
# ingress/api-ingress.yaml — one host, two paths, TLS, rate limit
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/part-of: jahez-api
  annotations:
    # ── controller behaviour for this Ingress only ──
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod-cluster-issuer
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "100"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections: "20"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/enable-cors: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/cors-allow-origin: "https://www.jahez.net"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "30"
spec:
  # ① Which controller should serve it?
  ingressClassName: nginx

  # ② Which requests? (host + path)
  rules:
    - host: api.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - # ③ Where to send /menu…?
            path: /menu
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port:
                  name: http
          - # ③ Where to send /orders…?
            path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-api-service
                port:
                  number: 80

  # ④ How is it secured?
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - api.jahez.net
      secretName: api-jahez-net-tls-secret

  # ⑤ What about everything else?
  defaultBackend:
    service:
      name: menu-api-service
      port:
        number: 80

3.1ingressClassName

In one sentence

ingressClassName picks which controller turns this Ingress into routes; no matching class means nothing happens.

Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
① Which controller?spec.ingressClassNamethe addressee

📄 ingress/class-examples.yamlyaml
# ingress/class-examples.yaml — the same app served by two controllers
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: menu-public-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which controller? → ingress-nginx
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: api.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /menu
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: { name: menu-api-service, port: { number: 80 } }
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: menu-internal-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internal
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip
spec:
  # ① Which controller? → AWS Load Balancer Controller (internal ALB for back-office)
  ingressClassName: alb
  rules:
    - host: menu.internal.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: { name: menu-api-service, port: { number: 80 } }

✕ When it fails
  • Class missing and no default class → no controller serves it; ADDRESS stays empty, no event.
  • Typo (ngnix) → same: silently unserved.
  • Both the annotation and the field set to different values → the API rejects the object.
② Which requests?

3.2rules · host

In one sentence

The host selects which server block handles the request; one Ingress can hold many hosts, and many Ingresses can share one host.

Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Which host?rules[].hostthe building
Which path?rules[].http.paths[].paththe floor
How strict?pathTypeexact flat or whole floor
host valueMatchesDoes not match
api.jahez.netapi.jahez.netAPI.jahez.net? (hosts are case-insensitive → matches) · www.api.jahez.net
*.preview.jahez.netpr-41.preview.jahez.netpreview.jahez.net · a.b.preview.jahez.net
(no host)every Host header, raw NLB name too—

📄 ingress/subdomains-ingress.yamlyaml
# ingress/subdomains-ingress.yaml — one subdomain per app, one wildcard certificate
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: subdomains-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "200"
spec:
  # ① Which controller?
  ingressClassName: nginx
  # ② Which requests?
  rules:
    - host: menu.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port: { number: 80 }
    - host: orders.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-api-service
                port: { number: 80 }
    - host: "*.preview.jahez.net"           # wildcard: one label only
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port: { number: 80 }
  # ④ Secured by one wildcard certificate (DNS-01, see §6.2)
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - menu.jahez.net
        - orders.jahez.net
        - "*.preview.jahez.net"
      secretName: wildcard-jahez-net-tls-secret

✕ When it fails
  • Two Ingresses with the same host + path → the admission webhook rejects the second (host "api.jahez.net" and path "/menu" is already defined).

3.3paths · pathType

In one sentence

pathType fixes how a path is compared: Exact for one URL, Prefix for a subtree, ImplementationSpecific for controller extras such as regex.

Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
How is the path compared?pathTypeexact flat · whole floor · building manager decides
Which path wins?longest match; Exact before Prefixmost specific address wins
pathTypepath/menu/menu//menu/items/menus/MENU
Exact/menu✓✕✕✕✕
Prefix/menu✓✓✓✕✕
Prefix/menu/✓✓✓✕✕
Prefix/✓✓✓✓✓
ImplementationSpecific + use-regex/menu(/|$)(.*)✓✓✓✕✕ (case-sensitive unless (?i))
📄 ingress/path-types-ingress.yamlyaml
# ingress/path-types-ingress.yaml — the three pathTypes side by side
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: path-types-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: api.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - # Exact: only /menu/health
            path: /menu/health
            pathType: Exact
            backend:
              service: { name: menu-api-service, port: { number: 80 } }
          - # Prefix: /menu and everything below it
            path: /menu
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: { name: menu-api-service, port: { number: 80 } }
          - # Prefix /: catch-all for this host (shortest, so it matches last)
            path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: { name: orders-api-service, port: { number: 80 } }

⚠ Trap

In ingress-nginx, once any path on a host uses use-regex or rewrite-target, all paths of that host become regex locations — a Prefix /menu can then also match /menu-old. Keep regex Ingresses on their own host or make the paths strict.

3.4backend · service

In one sentence

A backend names a Service and one of its ports; the controller resolves it to the Ready Pod IPs behind it and proxies there directly.

Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Which Service?backend.service.namethe flat
Which port?port.number or port.namethe door bell
Something else?backend.resourcea parcel locker instead of a flat

📄 apps/menu-api/service.yamlyaml
# apps/menu-api/service.yaml — internal only; the Ingress is the way in
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-api-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: menu-api
spec:
  type: ClusterIP              # not LoadBalancer — no NLB per app
  selector:
    app: menu-api
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http         # → containerPort 8080

    app.kubernetes.io/part-of: jahez-api
  annotations:
    # ── controller behaviour for this Ingress only ──
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod-cluster-issuer
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "100"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections: "20"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/enable-cors: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/cors-allow-origin: "https://www.jahez.net"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "30"
spec:
  # ① Which controller should serve it?
  ingressClassName: nginx

  # ② Which requests? (host + path)
  rules:
    - host: api.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - # ③ Where to send /menu…?
            path: /menu
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port:
                  name: http
          - # ③ Where to send /orders…?
            path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-api-service
                port:
                  number: 80

  # ④ How is it secured?
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - api.jahez.net
      secretName: api-jahez-net-tls-secret

  # ⑤ What about everything else?
  defaultBackend:
    service:
      name: menu-api-service
      port:
        number: 80

✕ When it fails
  • Served certificate is “Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate” → Secret missing, wrong namespace, or wrong type.
  • Browser warns about name mismatch → the host is not in the certificate’s SANs.
  • No HTTP→HTTPS redirect → the host is in rules but not in tls.hosts.

4.0How an IngressClass works

In one sentence

An IngressClass is a named pointer to one controller; Ingresses choose it by name, and at most one class should be the default.

Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
① Which controller implements it?spec.controllerthe company name on the post office
② Any extra settings?spec.parametersthe branch’s rule book
Default?annotation is-default-classwhere unaddressed letters go
Familynetworking.k8s.io/v1
Scopecluster
Created byHelm chart
Name herenginx (chart-owned)
📄 platform/ingress-nginx/ingress-class.yamlyaml
# What the chart creates from controller.ingressClassResource (shown for reference)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: IngressClass
metadata:
  name: nginx                                   # chart-owned name, kept as is
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx
  annotations:
    ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "false"
spec:
  # ① Which controller implements this class?
  controller: k8s.io/ingress-nginx
  # ② Extra controller settings (optional, controller-specific)
  # parameters:
  #   apiGroup: k8s.example.com
  #   kind: IngressParameters
  #   name: external-lb-parameters
  #   scope: Cluster

4.1The default IngressClass

In one sentence

The default class is written into an Ingress only when it is created without ingressClassName; existing Ingresses are not changed.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: IngressClass
metadata:
  name: nginx
  annotations:
    ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
spec:
  controller: k8s.io/ingress-nginx

Jahez choice

We keep default: false: every Ingress names its class. With two controllers (nginx + alb) a default hides mistakes. Two classes both marked default → creating a class-less Ingress fails.

4.2parameters

In one sentence

parameters points an IngressClass at a controller-specific settings object, so two classes of the same controller can behave differently.

📄 platform/aws-lbc/ingress-class-params.yamlyaml
# platform/aws-lbc/ingress-class-params.yaml — parameters example (AWS Load Balancer Controller)
apiVersion: elbv2.k8s.aws/v1beta1
kind: IngressClassParams
metadata:
  name: internal-alb-ingress-class-params
spec:
  scheme: internal
  group:
    name: jahez-internal
  loadBalancerAttributes:
    - key: idle_timeout.timeout_seconds
      value: "120"
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: IngressClass
metadata:
  name: alb-internal
spec:
  controller: ingress.k8s.aws/alb
  parameters:
    apiGroup: elbv2.k8s.aws
    kind: IngressClassParams
    name: internal-alb-ingress-class-params

4.3Installing ingress-nginx with Helm

In one sentence

One Helm release creates the controller Pods, its IngressClass, its admission webhook and one LoadBalancer Service — the only NLB the apps need.

The chart creates the Deployment, the LoadBalancer Service, the IngressClass, the ConfigMap, RBAC and the admission webhook. Everything Jahez-specific is in one values file.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: jahez-gitops → kubectl · helm → ingress-nginx controller Pods → ingress-nginx-controller → IngressClass nginx → admission webhook (inside the controller Pod)
📄 platform/ingress-nginx/values-prod.yamlyaml
# platform/ingress-nginx/values-prod.yaml
# helm upgrade --install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
#   -n ingress-nginx -f platform/ingress-nginx/values-prod.yaml --version 4.15.0
controller:
  # ① Which class does this controller own?
  ingressClass: nginx
  ingressClassResource:
    name: nginx                    # IngressClass object the chart creates
    enabled: true
    default: false                 # every Ingress must say ingressClassName: nginx
    controllerValue: k8s.io/ingress-nginx
  watchIngressWithoutClass: false

  # ② How many copies, and where?
  replicaCount: 3
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone    # me-central-1a/b/c
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx
          app.kubernetes.io/component: controller
  resources:
    requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
    limits: { memory: 512Mi }
  autoscaling:
    enabled: true
    minReplicas: 3
    maxReplicas: 9
    targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70

  # ③ How does traffic reach it? (one AWS NLB for the whole cluster)
  service:
    type: LoadBalancer
    externalTrafficPolicy: Local             # keep the client IP
    annotations:
      service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: external
      service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
      service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
      service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled: "true"

  # ④ Global behaviour (rendered into the controller ConfigMap)
  config:
    use-forwarded-headers: "true"
    hsts: "true"
    hsts-max-age: "31536000"
    proxy-body-size: 8m
    enable-real-ip: "true"
    log-format-escape-json: "true"
  allowSnippetAnnotations: false             # snippets stay off (CVE-2025-1974 family)

  # ⑤ Metrics for Prometheus / Grafana
  metrics:
    enabled: true
    serviceMonitor:
      enabled: true

⚠ Watch out

With Local and target type instance, nodes without a controller Pod fail health checks — use target type ip.

controller.service.annotationsobjectAWS LB Controller settings

Deep dive →

• controller.metrics.serviceMonitor.enabledboolean

4.15.0 / v1.15.0 is the final release. Pin it, keep allowSnippetAnnotations: false, keep the admission webhook internal, and track the migration in §1.4.

4.5Controller ConfigMap — global settings

In one sentence

The controller ConfigMap holds defaults for every Ingress; change it through Helm values, not by hand.

Global settings (all Ingresses) go into the controller ConfigMap through controller.config. Per-Ingress settings are annotations (§5.7). When both exist, the annotation wins for that Ingress.

📄 ConfigMap ingress-nginx-controlleryaml
# what the chart renders from controller.config
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: ingress-nginx-controller        # chart-owned name, kept as is
  namespace: ingress-nginx
data:
  use-forwarded-headers: "true"
  hsts: "true"
  hsts-max-age: "31536000"
  proxy-body-size: 8m
  enable-real-ip: "true"
  log-format-escape-json: "true"
KeyEffectPer-Ingress override
proxy-body-sizemax upload (413 above it)nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size
hstsStrict-Transport-Security header—
use-forwarded-headerstrust X-Forwarded-* from the NLB/CDN—
worker-shutdown-timeoutgraceful reload window—

Routing patterns

From simple to complex. Each pattern: diagram → full file → commands → real-shape output → result → when it fails.

5.0Patterns compared

In one sentence

Every pattern is the same Ingress object with a different mix of hosts, paths and annotations — pick by what differs between the backends.

PatternSplits byUse at JahezSection
Single servicenothinga back-office tool on its own host5.1
Path fan-outURL pathapi.jahez.net/menu, /orders5.2

5.1Single service

In one sentence

One host, one path /, one Service — the smallest useful Ingress.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Customer app → Ingress ×5 → menu-api-service
📄 ingress/backoffice-ingress.yamlyaml
# ingress/backoffice-ingress.yaml — one host, one Service
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: backoffice-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod-cluster-issuer
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/whitelist-source-range: "10.20.0.0/16,198.51.100.10/32"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: backoffice.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port: { number: 80 }
  tls:
    - hosts: [backoffice.jahez.net]
      secretName: backoffice-jahez-net-tls-secret

5.2Path fan-out

In one sentence

One host, several paths, each to a different Service — the main Jahez API pattern.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Customer app → Ingress ×5 → menu-api-service → orders-api-service
📄 ingress/api-ingress.yamlyaml
# ingress/api-ingress.yaml — one host, two paths, TLS, rate limit
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/part-of: jahez-api
  annotations:
    # ── controller behaviour for this Ingress only ──
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod-cluster-issuer
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "100"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections: "20"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/enable-cors: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/cors-allow-origin: "https://www.jahez.net"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "30"
spec:
  # ① Which controller should serve it?
  ingressClassName: nginx

  # ② Which requests? (host + path)
  rules:
    - host: api.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - # ③ Where to send /menu…?
            path: /menu
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port:
                  name: http
          - # ③ Where to send /orders…?
            path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-api-service
                port:
                  number: 80

  # ④ How is it secured?
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - api.jahez.net
      secretName: api-jahez-net-tls-secret

  # ⑤ What about everything else?
  defaultBackend:
    service:
      name: menu-api-service
      port:
        number: 80

5.3Name-based virtual hosts — different domains

In one sentence

Different domains on the same controller: each host gets its own server block and certificate.

5.4Subdomains and wildcard hosts

In one sentence

One subdomain per app plus a wildcard for preview environments, covered by a wildcard certificate from DNS-01.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Customer app → Ingress ×5 → menu-api-service → orders-api-service
📄 ingress/subdomains-ingress.yamlyaml
# ingress/subdomains-ingress.yaml — one subdomain per app, one wildcard certificate
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: subdomains-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "200"
spec:
  # ① Which controller?
  ingressClassName: nginx
  # ② Which requests?
  rules:
    - host: menu.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port: { number: 80 }
    - host: orders.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-api-service
                port: { number: 80 }
    - host: "*.preview.jahez.net"           # wildcard: one label only
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port: { number: 80 }
  # ④ Secured by one wildcard certificate (DNS-01, see §6.2)
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - menu.jahez.net
        - orders.jahez.net
        - "*.preview.jahez.net"
      secretName: wildcard-jahez-net-tls-secret

5.5Rewrite-target

In one sentence

A regex path captures parts of the URL and rewrite-target rebuilds the path the backend receives.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: Customer app → menu-api-service
📄 ingress/legacy-rewrite-ingress.yamlyaml
# ingress/legacy-rewrite-ingress.yaml — /v1/menu/<rest> reaches menu-api as /menu/<rest>
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: legacy-rewrite-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/use-regex: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /menu/$2
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: api.jahez.net
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /v1/menu(/|$)(.*)            # $1 = "/" or end, $2 = the rest
            pathType: ImplementationSpecific   # regex needs this type
            backend:
              service:
                name: menu-api-service
                port: { number: 80 }

5.6Canary — weight, header, cookie

In one sentence

A second Ingress with the same host + path and canary: "true" takes a share of the traffic, chosen by header, cookie or weight.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: orders-api-canary → Customer app → ingress-nginx controller Pods → orders-api-service
📄 apps/orders-api/canary.yamlyaml
# apps/orders-api/canary.yaml — v3.9.0 runs beside v3.8.1 with its own Service
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-api-canary-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-api
    track: canary
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-api
      track: canary
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders-api
        track: canary
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: orders-api
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/orders-api:3.9.0
          ports:
            - { name: http, containerPort: 8080 }
          env:
            - name: ASPNETCORE_PATHBASE
              value: /orders
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /orders/health/ready, port: http }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-api-canary-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: orders-api
    track: canary
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
📄 ingress/orders-canary-ingress.yamlyaml
# ingress/orders-canary-ingress.yaml — 5 % of /orders traffic goes to v3.9.0
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: orders-canary-ingress
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "5"
    # header wins over weight: QA sends X-Canary: always
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-header: X-Canary
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: api.jahez.net            # same host + path as api-ingress
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-api-canary-service
                port: { number: 80 }

5.7Annotations reference

In one sentence

Annotations switch on controller features per Ingress; they are strings, they are controller-specific, and typos are silently ignored.

Annotation (prefix nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/)ValueEffectExample
ssl-redirect"true"308 from http to httpskubectl annotate ing api-ingress -n jahez-prod nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect="true" --overwrite
force-ssl-redirect"true"redirect even without a tls block (TLS at the NLB)kubectl annotate ing api-ingress -n jahez-prod nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl-redirect="true"
limit-rps · limit-rpm"100"per client IP; burst = 5× (503 above)kubectl annotate ing api-ingress -n jahez-prod nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps="200" --overwrite
limit-connections"20"concurrent connections per IPkubectl annotate ing api-ingress -n jahez-prod nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections="50" --overwrite
enable-cors · cors-allow-origin"true" · origin listCORS headers + preflightkubectl annotate ing api-ingress -n jahez-prod nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/cors-allow-origin="https://www.jahez.net" --overwrite
proxy-body-size"8m"max request body (413)kubectl annotate ing api-ingress -n jahez-prod nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size="20m" --overwrite
proxy-read-timeout"30"seconds waiting for the app (504)kubectl annotate ing api-ingress -n jahez-prod nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout="60" --overwrite
whitelist-source-rangeCIDR listothers get 403kubectl annotate ing backoffice-ingress -n jahez-prod nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/whitelist-source-range="10.20.0.0/16" --overwrite
backend-protocolHTTP · HTTPS · GRPCprotocol to the Podkubectl annotate ing api-ingress -n jahez-prod nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol="GRPC"
affinity · session-cookie-name"cookie"sticky sessionskubectl annotate ing api-ingress -n jahez-prod nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/affinity="cookie"
auth-urlURLexternal auth sub-request (401/403)kubectl annotate ing backoffice-ingress -n jahez-prod nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-url="http://auth-service.jahez-prod.svc/verify"
configuration-snippetnginx configdisabled (allowSnippetAnnotations: false) — security risk—
⚠ Watch out
  • Values are strings: "true", "100". YAML true without quotes is rejected.
  • A misspelled annotation is ignored silently — check the rendered nginx.conf.
  • Annotations are the part that does not move to another controller.
6

TLS with cert-manager

Issuer → Certificate → Secret → Ingress, and how renewals happen without anyone noticing.

6.0How TLS flows

In one sentence

You declare an issuer and the names; cert-manager proves domain ownership to Let’s Encrypt, writes the TLS Secret and renews it before it expires.

⎈ Full cluster · After Ingress — one NLB, ingress-nginx Pods route by host + path
↔ swipe the diagram · ⤢ full screen
Lit: ClusterIssuer → Ingress ×5 → Certificate → Let’s Encrypt → TLS Secrets → ingress-nginx controller Pods
ObjectWho writes itPurpose
ClusterIssueryou (platform)CA + how to solve challenges
Certificateyou, or cert-manager from the Ingress annotationwhich names, which Secret
CertificateRequest · Order · Challengecert-managerone issuance attempt and its proof
Secret (kubernetes.io/tls)cert-managerthe result the Ingress uses

6.1ClusterIssuer

In one sentence

A ClusterIssuer is the cluster-wide account with a certificate authority plus the rules for proving you own each domain.

Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
① Which certificate authority?acme.server · email · privateKeySecretRefwhich notary
② How do we prove the domain?solvers[] (http01 · dns01 · selector)show your ID: a file on the website, or a DNS record
📄 platform/cert-manager/cluster-issuer.yamlyaml
# platform/cert-manager/cluster-issuer.yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod-cluster-issuer
spec:
  acme:
    # ① Which certificate authority?
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: platform@jahez.net
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-account-key-secret
    # ② How do we prove we own the domain?
    solvers:
      - http01:                          # single hosts: api.jahez.net …
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: nginx
      - selector:
          dnsZones:
            - jahez.net                  # wildcards need DNS-01
        dns01:
          route53:
            region: me-central-1
            hostedZoneID: Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ
